In [[commutative algebra]], an '''N-1 ring''' is an [[integral domain]] <math>A</math> whose [[integral closure]] in its [[quotient field]] is a [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] <math>A</math>-[[module (mathematics)|module]]. It is called a '''Japanese ring''' (or an '''N-2 ring''') if for every [[finite extension]] <math>L</math> of its quotient field <math>K</math>, the integral closure of <math>A</math> in <math>L</math> is a finitely generated <math>A</math>-module (or equivalently a finite <math>A</math>-[[algebra over a ring|algebra]]). A [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] is called '''universally Japanese''' if every finitely generated integral domain over it is Japanese, and is called a '''Nagata ring''', named for [[Masayoshi Nagata]], or a '''pseudo-geometric ring''' if it is [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] and universally Japanese (or, which turns out to be the same, if it is Noetherian and all of its [[quotient ring|quotients]] by a [[prime ideal]] are N-2 rings). A ring is called '''geometric''' if it is the [[local ring]] of an [[algebraic variety]] or a [[completion of a ring|completion]] of such a local ring,<ref>{{harv|Danilov|2001}}</ref> but this concept is not used much.

==Examples==

[[Field (mathematics)|Fields]] and rings of [[polynomial]]s or [[formal power series|power series]] in finitely many indeterminates over fields are examples of Japanese rings. Another important example is a Noetherian [[integrally closed domain]] (e.g. a [[Dedekind domain]]) having a [[Perfect field|perfect]] [[field of fractions]]. On the other hand, a [[principal ideal domain]] or even a [[discrete valuation ring]] is not necessarily Japanese.

Any [[quasi-excellent ring]] is a Nagata ring, so in particular almost all Noetherian rings that occur in [[algebraic geometry]] are Nagata rings.
The first example of a Noetherian domain that is not a Nagata ring was given by {{harvtxt|Akizuki|1935}}.

Here is an example of a discrete valuation ring that is not a Japanese ring. Choose a prime <math>p</math> and an infinite [[degree of a field extension|degree]] [[field extension]] <math>K</math> of a [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] <math>p</math> field <math>k</math>, such that <math>K^p\subseteq k</math>. Let the discrete valuation ring <math>R</math> be the [[ring of formal power series]] over <math>K</math> whose coefficients generate a finite extension of <math>k</math>. If <math>y</math> is any formal power series not in <math>R</math> then the ring <math>R[y]</math> is not an N-1 ring (its integral closure is not a finitely generated module) so <math>R</math> is not a Japanese ring.

If <math>R</math> is the [[subring]] of the [[polynomial ring]] <math>k[x_1, x_2, ...]</math> in infinitely many generators generated by the squares and cubes of all generators, and <math>S</math> is obtained from <math>R</math> by adjoining inverses to all elements not in any of the [[ideal (ring theory)|ideals]] generated by some <math>x_n</math>, then <math>S</math> is a {{nowrap|1-dimensional}} Noetherian domain that is not an N-1 ring, in other words its integral closure in its quotient field is not a finitely generated <math>S</math>-module. Also <math>S</math> has a cusp singularity at every [[closed point]], so the set of singular points is not closed.
